content: 1. The authors concluded that in Taiwan, China, syndromic management of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) was more cost-effective than etiological diagnosis when considering the cost per person treated from a healthcare provider's perspective. This conclusion was influenced by the prevalence of genital ulcer disease caused by pathogens such as Haemophilus ducreyi and HSV-2. 2. Syndromic management is likely to be cost-saving in rural South Africa due to its potential impact on reducing HIV incidence. 3. The cost of antiviral agents may be prohibitively high for some individuals or in certain settings. Similarly, the overall cost of STI management, including consultation, drugs, and diagnostic tests, may be unaffordable for specific subpopulations. 4. Diagnostic tests for genital ulcers, such as multiplex polymerase chain reaction (M-PCR), are expensive, technically complex, and time-consuming. As a result, they are often inaccessible or unavailable in resource-limited settings. 5. In Peru, clinicians and pharmacies offered syndromic management in a community-randomized controlled trial. In Pakistan, over 90% of 100 clinicians expressed willingness to attend educational sessions and adhere to national STI treatment protocols. 6. Concerns have been raised about the treatment of genital ulcer disease by general practitioners in Namibia. Similarly, healthcare providers in Karachi, including doctors and midwives, reported challenges in delivering syndromic STI management. 7. In the United Republic of Tanzania, 83% of patients reported satisfaction with STI services using syndromic management. However, healthcare providers may face difficulties in discussing sensitive sexual health issues, and symptomatic patients may not disclose their symptoms due to stigma, lack of access, or other reasons. 8. Immediate symptom relief is often preferred by patients over waiting for test results. 9. Syndromic management of genital ulcer disease has been implemented with varying success in resource-limited settings, including Ethiopia, Kenya, Malawi, Peru, India, Zambia, Namibia, China, Zimbabwe, South Africa, Bangladesh, Burkina Faso, Brazil, the Central African Republic, Rwanda, Côte d’Ivoire, Swaziland, Gambia, and Mozambique. 10. In the United Republic of Tanzania, standardized simulated patients visiting pharmacies found challenges in the adequate management of genital ulcer disease syndromes. Similarly, pharmacy staff in Gambia were willing to offer syndromic management, but none of the simulated patients with genital ulcer disease received appropriate treatment. 11. In rural South African clinics, only 9% of cases were correctly managed using a syndromic management approach. A survey of 43 doctors in South Africa revealed that only 23% had correct knowledge of managing genital ulcer disease. 12. In Namibia, none of the 50 general practitioners interviewed could properly manage genital ulcer disease according to syndromic management guidelines. In six West African countries, effective STI treatment was provided to only 14% of patients across 240 healthcare facilities. 13. Community pharmacies in South Africa see many potential STI cases, but none of the 85 head pharmacists correctly identified the treatment for genital ulcers. In Rwanda, nurses in country towns were able to deliver syndromic STI management. 14. In India, syndromic management protocols were followed for 70% of genital ulcer disease cases presenting to a male health clinic. A study in South Africa found that only 14% of general practitioners in the private sector reported effective treatment for genital ulcer disease. 15. A mixed-methods study in Ethiopia involving 250 clinicians, including mystery patients, found that only 13% were trained in syndromic STI management, highlighting the need for training and supervision. In Nigeria, 16 nurses from primary health centers were trained to manage STIs using a syndromic approach, demonstrating its feasibility and acceptability. 16. Doctors and paramedics in India were successfully trained for syndromic case management. Syndromic management is often provided at the primary care level, including pharmacies, in lowand middle-income countries without clinical examination. 17. A syndromic algorithm may be preferable to no intervention, allowing healthcare providers to make rapid diagnoses without requiring specialized skills or sophisticated laboratory investigations. 18. Scaling up syndromic management requires adequate training and supervision. Regular updates to syndromic management protocols are necessary to reflect changing STI trends, and ongoing evaluation of service quality is essential, including adherence to algorithms. 19. Periodic etiological diagnosis is needed to monitor changes in the epidemiology of STIs causing syndromes and to determine whether prescribed antibiotics need to be adjusted. 20. For individuals presenting with genital ulcers, treatment based on quality-assured molecular assays of the ulcer is recommended. In settings with limited or no molecular testing capacity, syndromic treatment should be provided to ensure same-day treatment. 21. Good clinical practice includes taking a medical and sexual history, assessing STI risk, performing a physical examination of the genital and anal areas, offering HIV and syphilis testing, and providing analgesics for pain. 22. In settings with quality-assured molecular testing, molecular assays (NAAT) should be performed on anogenital lesions to confirm or exclude herpes simplex virus and Treponema pallidum (syphilis). Treatment should be based on same-day results or managed syndromically until results are available. 23. Treatment for chancroid should only be provided in geographical settings where cases are reported or emerging. Persistent anogenital ulcers should be referred to centers with laboratory capacity and expertise to diagnose less common pathogens or other conditions. 24. Genital ulcer disease refers to breaks in the skin or mucosa, presenting as ulcers, sores, or vesicles. Anogenital ulcers are located in the genital or anal areas and may be painful or painless. 25. A negative serological test for syphilis in the presence of anogenital ulcers lasting less than three weeks does not definitively exclude syphilis, as antibodies may not yet be detectable. 26. Syndromic management of anogenital ulcers results in small benefits and moderate harms compared to molecular testing or treating all cases. Molecular testing may not be feasible in all settings, and treating all cases is a feasible and low-cost alternative. 27. Treating all cases or conducting molecular testing is acceptable to all stakeholders and may increase equity in some settings.
